post.title: Ben Simmons — achilles rupture
post.markdown_body:
## The Snapshot

Per the Sacramento Kings, Ben Simmons tore his right Achilles tendon in practice this week, days before the season opener, ending a comeback attempt that began with a one-year minimum contract. It is the latest in a long run of injuries, most notably to his back, that has kept him off the court for much of the last several seasons.

## What Happened

According to the Kings, Simmons was hurt during a live drill in practice on Sunday. The Kings confirmed a torn right Achilles tendon, per the team's statement, and said surgery was completed on Tuesday October 20. ESPN's Shams Charania reported the injury first. Simmons signed with Sacramento in September 2026 after missing most of recent seasons. He has said publicly that he has been knocked down before and has always gotten back up.

The injury lands on a long medical history. In 2016 he fractured his right foot, the same side, in a scrimmage before his rookie season and had surgery to repair it.  He subsequently missed that entire year. Per public reporting he has since had a lower back nerve impingement, a knee injury, a herniated disc, a back surgery, and a recurrence of the nerve problem shut him down after 15 games in 2023-24. Reporting on exact dates and procedures is not consistent, so this account follows the public record only.

The surgeon, the surgical approach and the team's own recovery estimate have not been released.

## The Anatomy

The Achilles is the largest tendon in the body. It connects the calf muscles to the heel bone and carries the force of every push-off, jump and sprint. Complete tears usually happen in the middle of the tendon or near its heel attachment, often during a sudden push-off or change of direction, which is consistent with a live practice drill. Tendons that have been repeatedly loaded or have gone through long layoffs can be less forgiving, although a single report cannot say whether that applies here.

## The Repair

A complete tear in an elite athlete is most often treated with surgical repair, followed by a staged rehabilitation: a period of protection, gradual weight bearing, calf strengthening, then running, jumping and cutting before basketball. The team has said surgery has been completed.The surgical technique used is not known.

## The Timeline

Surgery was reported complete on Tuesday October 20, so the clock has started. Recovery from an Achilles tear is generally measured in many months, not weeks. Return to full competitive basketball commonly takes around nine to twelve months or longer, and strength and explosiveness can lag behind the date an athlete is cleared. The Kings have not published a return timeline, so any date should be treated as an estimate.

For Simmons, the backdrop matters. He would be rebuilding the calf, tendon and push-off mechanics while also managing a back with a long surgical and nerve history, and he has not played a full season in years. That does not predict how this recovery will go. It does mean the rehabilitation has more moving parts than it would for an athlete with a clean medical record. Dated updates will be added as they are reported.

## Why It Matters For You

Achilles tears are not only a professional athlete's injury. They are common in recreational players in their 30s and 40s, often in a sudden push-off after a stretch of inactivity or a return to play. If you feel a pop or a sudden sharp blow at the back of the ankle, followed by weakness pushing off, get it examined promptly. Early assessment affects the treatment options.

## Dr. Johnson's Take

What stands out to me is the sequence. A player coming back from multiple publicly reported injuries enters a preseason ramp-up, then suffers a reported tendon injury in a drill. I cannot claim a link between his prior problems and this tear, although the frequency of injury is noteworthy. What I can say is that the first season back after a long layoff is a stress test for the body, and tendons are one of the slowest tissues to adapt.

---

Commentary by Keith P. Johnson, MD is general educational analysis based on publicly reported information. Dr. Johnson has not examined or treated these athletes. This is not a diagnosis, not medical advice, and does not create a physician-patient relationship.
